title: Probability & Random Variables
sub: Lecture 7 · events, probability rules, random variables & moments
blurb: Random experiments, classical and statistical probability, conditional probability, discrete and continuous random variables, distribution functions, expected value and variance.
lede: Probability gives us a numerical way to reason about uncertainty. This lecture builds from basic events and probability rules to discrete and continuous random variables, their distribution functions, quantiles, expected value and variance.
six: A **random event** A has probability 0 < P(A) < 1; a **certain event** E has P(E) = 1 and an **impossible event** Ø has P(Ø) = 0.
**Classical probability** is P(A) = m / n (requires equally likely outcomes); **statistical probability** approximates P(A) by relative frequency f / n as trials n grow.
Two events are **independent** when P(A|B) = P(A); **disjoint** events have A ∩ B = Ø and P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).
A **discrete** random variable uses probability function P(x) (sums to 1), while a **continuous** random variable uses density f(x) (integrates to 1, and P(X = x) = 0).
The **cumulative distribution function** F(x) = P(X ≤ x) works for both types: it is non-decreasing from 0 to 1 and gives range probabilities via F(x₂) - F(x₁).
**Expected value** E(X) measures the level (centre) of a distribution, while **variance** Var(X) = E(X²) - [E(X)]² and **standard deviation** S.D.(X) = √Var(X) measure its spread.
must: Probability rules, F(x) & expected value / variance
foot: Source: 4ST601 Lecture slides (7-time-series-seasonal.txt: Probability & Random Variables).

questions.q: What are the probabilities of a certain event E and an impossible event Ø?
questions.h: One always happens under given conditions; the other can never happen.
questions.e: A certain event E occurs with probability 1 (100%), an impossible event Ø has probability 0, and a random event A has 0 < P(A) < 1.

questions.q: Two events A and A' are complementary when:
questions.h: They cannot happen together AND together they cover all outcomes.
questions.answer: A ∩ A' = Ø and A ∪ A' = E, so P(A) + P(A') = 1
wrong: A ∩ A' ≠ Ø and P(A) + P(A') = 1
A ∪ A' = Ø and P(A) = P(A')
questions.e: Complementary events are disjoint (A ∩ A' = Ø) and together include all outcomes of the experiment (A ∪ A' = E), giving P(A) = 1 - P(A').

questions.q: When can we use the classical definition of probability P(A) = m / n?
questions.h: Think about what we assume before running the random experiment.
questions.answer: When all n possible outcomes of the experiment are equally likely
wrong: Only after repeating the experiment at least 600 times
Whenever the outcomes are continuous real numbers
Only when the events are mutually exclusive
questions.e: The classical definition P(A) = m / n assumes before the random experiment that all n possible outcomes are equally likely.

questions.q: A six-sided die is rolled 600 times in a casino and the number 6 falls 50 times. Using the statistical definition, what is the estimated probability of rolling a 6?
questions.h: Divide the number of occurrences f by the number of trials n.
questions.answer: 50 / 600 ≈ 0.083 (about 8.3%), suggesting the die is not fair
questions.e: By the statistical (frequentist) definition, P(A) ≈ f / n = 50 / 600 ≈ 0.083 (8.3%), which differs from 1/6 ≈ 17% and indicates the die is not fair.

questions.q: Two events A and B are independent if and only if:
questions.h: Knowing B occurred does not change the probability of A.
questions.e: Independence means the occurrence of one event does not influence the probability of the other: P(A|B) = P(A) and P(B|A) = P(B).

questions.q: Rolling a fair six-sided die once, A = {2, 4, 6} (even) and B = {4, 5, 6} (> 3). What is P(A|B) and are A and B independent?
questions.h: Restrict the outcomes to B = {4, 5, 6}, then see how many are even.
questions.answer: P(A|B) = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 ≠ P(A) = 0.5, so A and B are dependent
wrong: P(A|B) = 1/2 = 0.5 = P(A), so A and B are independent
P(A|B) = 1/3 ≈ 0.33 ≠ P(A), so A and B are dependent
P(A|B) = 2/6 = 0.33, so A and B are disjoint
questions.e: Given B = {4, 5, 6} (3 outcomes), two outcomes are even (4 and 6), so P(A|B) = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 ≠ 0.5 = P(A). Therefore A and B are dependent.

questions.q: A bank has two independent alarm systems with detection probabilities P(A) = 0.9 and P(B) = 0.8. What is the probability that at least one detects a burglary?
questions.h: Use the general addition rule: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A ∩ B).
questions.e: Because A and B are independent, P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B) = 0.9·0.8 = 0.72. Thus P(A ∪ B) = 0.9 + 0.8 - 0.72 = 0.98 (98%).

questions.q: Which formula is the general multiplication rule for two dependent events A and B?
questions.h: One probability is multiplied by a conditional probability.
questions.answer: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B|A) = P(B) · P(A|B)
questions.e: For dependent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A)·P(B|A) = P(B)·P(A|B). Only for independent events does this simplify to P(A)·P(B).

questions.q: What distinguishes a discrete random variable from a continuous random variable?
questions.h: Compare the set of possible values each can take.
questions.answer: A discrete RV has a finite or countably infinite number of values; a continuous RV can take any value within one or more intervals
wrong: A discrete RV can only take 0 or 1; a continuous RV takes any integer
A discrete RV uses f(x); a continuous RV uses P(x)
A discrete RV has F(+∞) = 1; a continuous RV has F(+∞) = ∞
questions.e: A discrete RV has finite or countably infinite values, whereas a continuous RV can take any value within one or more intervals (infinitely many values).

questions.q: How is the cumulative distribution function F(x) defined for both discrete and continuous random variables?
questions.h: It accumulates probability up to and including x.
questions.e: For both discrete and continuous random variables, F(x) = P(X ≤ x), with 0 ≤ F(x) ≤ 1, F(-∞) = 0, and F(+∞) = 1.

questions.q: For a continuous random variable X, what is P(X = x) at any single point x?
questions.h: A single point has zero width under a density curve.
questions.answer: Always 0, so P(X < x) = P(X ≤ x)
wrong: Equal to the cumulative probability F(x)
questions.e: For any continuous RV, P(X = x) = 0 for all x ∈ (-∞, +∞), which is why P(X < x) = P(X ≤ x).

questions.q: For the siblings distribution P(0)=0.40, P(1)=0.35, P(2)=0.15, P(3)=0.07, P(4)=0.03, what is P(1 < X < 4)?
questions.e: The values strictly between 1 and 4 are x = 2 and x = 3, so P(1 < X < 4) = P(2) + P(3) = 0.15 + 0.07 = 0.22.

questions.q: Given the density f(x) = 2x for 0 < x < 1 (and 0 otherwise), what is F(x) for 0 < x < 1 and what is P(1/3 < X ≤ 2/3)?
questions.h: Integrate 2t from 0 to x to get F(x), then compute F(2/3) - F(1/3).
questions.e: Integrating f(t) = 2t from 0 to x gives F(x) = x² for 0 < x < 1. Then F(2/3) - F(1/3) = (2/3)² - (1/3)² = 4/9 - 1/9 = 3/9 = 1/3.

questions.q: For the siblings distribution (x = 0..4 with P = 0.4, 0.35, 0.15, 0.07, 0.03), what are E(X) and Var(X)?
questions.h: E(X) = Σ x·P(x) and Var(X) = Σ x²·P(x) - [E(X)]².

questions.q: Using the siblings distribution (F(0)=0.40 for 0≤x<1, F(1)=0.75 for 1≤x<2, F(2)=0.90 for 2≤x<3, F(3)=0.97 for 3≤x<4), what are the lower quartile x₀.₂₅ and 95% quantile x₀.₉₅?
questions.h: Find where F(x) first reaches or exceeds P.
questions.e: At x = 0, F jumps to 0.40 (exceeding 0.25), so x₀.₂₅ = 0. At x = 3, F jumps from 0.90 to 0.97 (crossing 0.95), so x₀.₉₅ = 3.

questions.q: For the continuous RV with F(x) = x² on (0, 1), what is the lower quartile x₀.₂₅?
questions.e: From F(x₀.₂₅) = x² = 0.25 (on 0 < x < 1), taking the positive square root gives x₀.₂₅ = √0.25 = 0.5.

vocab.meaning: A process that, when carried out, results in one of two or more possible outcomes.
An experiment whose outcome cannot be predicted with certainty and can yield different outcomes under the same conditions.
A single particular result of an experiment.
A collection of one or more outcomes of an experiment, denoted by capital letters A, B, etc.
An event guaranteed to occur under given conditions, with P(E) = 1.
An event that cannot occur under given conditions, with P(Ø) = 0.
Mutually exclusive events whose intersection is empty (A ∩ B = Ø).
Two disjoint events A and A' whose union is the certain event E, so P(A) + P(A') = 1.
P(A) = m / n, assuming all n possible outcomes are equally likely before the experiment.
Estimating P(A) by the relative frequency f / n over a large number of repetitions n.
The probability P(A|B) that event A occurs given that event B has already occurred.
Events where the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other: P(A|B) = P(A).
A variable whose numerical value is determined by the outcome of a random experiment.
A random variable with a finite or countably infinite number of possible values.
A random variable that can take any value within one or more intervals (infinitely many values).
For a discrete RV, P(x) = P(X = x), with 0 ≤ P(x) ≤ 1 and Σ P(x) = 1.
For a continuous RV, the derivative f(x) = F'(x) with f(x) ≥ 0 and total integral 1.
The cumulative probability F(x) = P(X ≤ x) for any real x.
The characteristic of the level (centre) of a distribution: Σ x·P(x) or ∫ x·f(x) dx.
A measure of spread around E(X), computed as E(X²) - [E(X)]².
The square root of the variance: √Var(X).
The value x_P where F(x_P) = P(X < x_P) = P, separating the lower 100·P% of values.

facts: A certain event E has probability {1|0|0.5|-1}.
Two events with an empty intersection A ∩ B = Ø are called {disjoint|independent|complementary|conditional}.
For complementary events A and A', P(A) equals {1 - P(A')|P(A')|1 + P(A')|0}.
The classical definition P(A) = m / n assumes all outcomes are {equally likely|independent|continuous|disjoint}.
Two events A and B are independent when P(A|B) equals {P(A)|P(B)|0|1 - P(A)}.
For any two events, P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) - {P(A ∩ B)|P(A)·P(B) only|P(A|B)|1}.
For a continuous random variable, the probability P(X = x) at any single value is always {0|1|f(x)|F(x)}.
The cumulative distribution function F(x) is defined as {P(X ≤ x)|P(X = x)|P(X > x)|f(x)}.
For f(x) = 2x on 0 < x < 1, the distribution function on that interval is {x²|2x|x/2|2}.
Variance is computed as E(X²) minus {[E(X)]²|E(X)|S.D.(X)|P(x)}.
Standard deviation S.D.(X) is the {square root|square|reciprocal|derivative} of Var(X).
